source_text: De habitu uero dumtaxat feminarum uarietas obseruationis effecit post sanctissimum apostolum nos uel maxime nullius loci homines impudenter retractare, nisi quod non impudenter, si secundum apostolum retractemus. de modestia quidem cultus et ornatus aperta praescriptio est etiam Petri, cohibentis eodem ore, quia eodem et spiritu, quo Paulus, et uestium gloriam et auri superbiam et crinium lenonem operositatem.
thought_title: The Variety of Observance About Women's Dress
orientation: Tertullian is beginning his discussion of the customs of prayer, and here he turns to the question of women's dress and adornment, saying that after the apostle Paul's teaching it is shameful for Christians to reopen the matter.
pass_a_gloss: But concerning the dress of women only, the variety of observance has caused us, after the most holy apostle, to reconsider shamelessly, we who are men of no place at all, except that it is not shameless, if we reconsider according to the apostle. Concerning the modesty of attire and adornment, there is an open prescription also of Peter, who restrains with the same mouth, because also with the same spirit as Paul, both the glory of clothing and the pride of gold and the pimping laboriousness of hair.

choices.english: men of no place at all
choices.why: Keeps the self-deprecating literal sense: people of no standing or position, which is the force of the Latin phrase.
Preserves the adverb's force and the verb's sense of going over a matter again, matching Tertullian's rhetorical self-accusation.
Keeps the harsh metaphor of leno as pimp and the literal operositas as laboriousness, which is Tertullian's point about elaborate hair-dressing.
Renders aperta as open or clear and praescriptio as prescription, matching the legal tone of a rule laid down.

bible_refs.note: Peter's teaching against outward adornment, gold, and braided hair is referenced but not quoted verbatim.
Paul's similar teaching on women's modest dress and adornment is in view as the apostolic prescription.

pass_b_english: But as for the dress of women, differences in practice have led us, people of no standing at all, to reconsider the matter after the most holy apostle. We do so shamelessly, except that it is not shameless if we reconsider it according to the apostle. On the modesty of attire and adornment there is indeed an open prescription, even from Peter. With the same mouth, because with the same Spirit as Paul, he restrains the glory of clothing, the pride of gold, and the seductive elaborateness of hair.

problems.quote: variety of practice has led us—men of no place at all—to reconsider the matter
problems.why: 'Men of no place at all' is opaque; likely means 'of no standing' or 'insignificant men'.
problems.fix: Render: 'men of no authority' or 'insignificant as we are'.

problems.why: 'Pimping' is jarring and unclear; likely means 'elaborate' or 'seductive' styling.
problems.fix: Use 'seductive elaborateness of hair' or 'ostentatious styling of hair'.

fixed: Changed 'men of no place at all' to 'men of no standing at all' to clarify 'nullius loci homines' as men of no rank or authority.
Changed 'the pimping laboriousness of hair' to 'the seductive elaborateness of hair' to render 'crinium lenonem operositatem' more clearly as the seductive, elaborate styling of hair.

problems.quote: variety of practice has led us, men of no standing at all, to reconsider the matter after the most holy apostle, and to do so shamelessly, except that it is not shameless if we reconsider it according to the apostle.
problems.why: The sentence is convoluted and self-cancelling; 'men of no standing' and 'shamelessly…not shameless' confuse.
problems.fix: Rephrase: 'Though we are men of no standing, we dare to reconsider the matter after the apostle—not shamelessly, but following him.'

fixed: The English accurately renders the source's concessive structure: 'uarietas obseruationis effecit... impudenter retractare, nisi quod non impudenter, si secundum apostolum retractemus.' The sentence is deliberately self-cancelling in the Latin, and the English preserves that. I changed only the comma to a dash to clarify the concessive turn, without altering the meaning.

dismissed.why: The Latin refers to elaborate or ornate hair styling, not to 'pimping' or a notion of laboriousness; the English adds a modern, inaccurate sense.
dismissed.note: 'Lenonem operositatem' is a pandering, laborious fuss, so the literal rendering is fair. The proposed 'elaborate hairdressing' drops the metaphor.

polish.changed: Clarified the phrase 'men of no place at all' to 'men of no standing at all' and smoothed the sentence structure for easier reading.
